module_title: British Policies - Stages of Colonialism, Railways, and Famine Commissions
introduction: This advanced level provides a critical analysis of the three stages of British colonialism (as classified by R.P. Dutt), the imperial motives behind railway expansion (Guarantee System), and the devastating famines coupled with the colonial response via Famine Commissions.

core_concepts.title: Three Stages of Colonialism (by R.P. Dutt)
core_concepts.description:
1. Mercantilism (1757-1813): Monopoly trade and direct plunder.
2. Free Trade (1813-1858): India became a dumping ground for British industrial goods and an exporter of raw materials.
3. Financial Imperialism (1858-1947): Investment of British capital in India (railways, banking, plantations) to earn massive guaranteed profits.

core_concepts.title: Railways and the Guarantee System
core_concepts.description: Railways were introduced under Lord Dalhousie in 1853 primarily to transport raw materials to ports and move troops quickly. Under the 'Guarantee System', British investors were promised a fixed 5% interest on their investments, the burden of which fell entirely on Indian taxpayers.

core_concepts.title: Financial Decentralization
core_concepts.description: Initiated by Lord Mayo in 1870, this policy granted some financial autonomy to provincial governments. It was later expanded by Lord Lytton and Lord Ripon to streamline colonial administration.

core_concepts.title: Famines and British Policies
core_concepts.description: Over-taxation and forced cultivation of cash crops led to severe famines. The British formed several Famine Commissions: Campbell (1866), Strachey (1880), Lyall (1897), and MacDonnell (1900). The Strachey Commission recommended the creation of a 'Famine Code'.

core_concepts.title: Nature of Foreign Capital Investment
core_concepts.description: British capital was strategically invested only in export-oriented sectors (plantations, railways, shipping) that benefited the British economy. They deliberately discouraged the development of heavy machinery or capital goods industries in India.

important_entities.name: Rajani Palme Dutt (R.P. Dutt)
important_entities.significance: In his famous book 'India Today', he provided a sharp and precise analysis of the three stages of British economic exploitation.

important_entities.name: Lord Dalhousie
important_entities.significance: Introduced Railways, Telegraphs, modern Postal systems, and the PWD, though the underlying motive was strictly to tighten the British imperial grip.

important_entities.name: Richard Strachey
important_entities.significance: Appointed under Lord Lytton, this commission officially recognized that it was the duty of the state to provide employment and food relief during famines.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Colonial historians view railways as a gift of modernization. However, Indian nationalists (like Tilak and G.V. Joshi) described it as 'decorating another's wife', because it was built using Indian money exclusively for British strategic and economic benefit.
The 'Free Trade' policy post-1813 was completely one-sided. While British goods entered India duty-free, Indian manufactured goods faced prohibitive import duties (often over 100%) in Britain.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: An easy acronym to remember the correct chronological order of the major British Famine Commissions.

exam_strategy_tips: UPSC frequently asks for the names and timelines of R.P. Dutt's three stages of colonialism.
In Assertion-Reasoning questions, clearly link the 'Guarantee System' of the railways to the broader concept of the 'Drain of Wealth'.
